strengths: The paper introduces a compelling and underexplored computer-vision problem: constructing controllable 3D head avatars from lifelong, unstructured photo collections. I assess it primarily as an Algorithms/General contribution, with a secondary Datasets/Benchmarks contribution.

TimeWalker combines a shared canonical representation, life-stage-dependent neural bases, and FLAME-driven dynamic 2D Gaussian surfels into a coherent system supporting rendering, expression transfer, viewpoint changes, and mesh extraction.

The reported image metrics are strong. On the evaluated TimeWalker-1.0 subset, the single lifelong model substantially outperforms adapted INSTA, FlashAvatar, and INSTA++ under the 1-vs-1 protocol, while remaining competitive with per-stage models under the more favorable 1-vs-N baseline protocol.

The paper includes extensive supplementary material, several baseline families, component ablations, compute information, qualitative failure cases, and candid discussion of limitations such as large-view artifacts, unseen mouth regions, imperfect lighting disentanglement, and preprocessing dependence.

The proposed TimeWalker-1.0 collection is potentially valuable: 40 identities and 2.7M frames spanning multiple life stages would provide a useful testbed if it can be released with sufficiently clear provenance, permissions, annotations, and evaluation splits.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol risks serious leakage. Taking the last 10% of frames from each appearance as test data can place near-duplicate or temporally adjacent frames from the same source video in training and testing. No video-level, event-level, or source-level separation is described. Consequently, the excellent reconstruction metrics may primarily measure interpolation or memorization rather than generalization to unseen photographs, poses, or life stages.

The central lifelong-generalization claims are not directly validated. Experiments use only 5 of the 40 identities, ablations use 3, and there is no held-out-life-stage experiment, age interpolation benchmark with ground truth, or systematic test of identity preservation across unseen ages. The ArcFace evaluation covers only three identities and one one-shot baseline, which is insufficient evidence for long-horizon identity consistency.

The claimed disentanglement is mostly supported by selected qualitative examples. There are no quantitative tests of cross-stage expression transfer, shape control, or factor leakage. The paper itself shows that residual embeddings mix lighting with life-stage identity, while extreme expressions and unseen mouth content fail. Thus, the evidence supports controllable reconstruction at observed stages more convincingly than a genuinely disentangled lifelong parametric space.

Geometry evidence is particularly weak. Mesh quality is assessed almost entirely through qualitative renderings without ground-truth geometry, Chamfer distance, normal error, or temporal-consistency measurements. Moreover, Colmap and Gaussian Surfels receive a single stage while TimeWalker receives all stages, confounding the claimed advantage of DNA-2DGS with additional data and head priors.

Several technical details are underspecified or questionable for reproducibility. Gaussian rotations are presented as being additively updated despite quaternion constraints, and the paper does not clearly explain how the affine/Frenet transformation updates surfel orientation and scale or handles nearest-triangle discontinuities. Important preprocessing details, life-stage grouping rules, baseline tuning, and the construction of fair camera/expression splits are also missing.

Dynamo's empirical advantage over fixed-capacity alternatives is modest: compared with all or 20 hashgrids, gains are only about 0.26–0.34 dB PSNR, with essentially tied LPIPS. The paper does not report model size, retained bases for all identities, sensitivity to the pruning threshold, or a quality-memory Pareto analysis, so claims of compactness, interpretability, and scalability are only partially supported.

Originality is moderate rather than decisive: the method largely combines established 2D Gaussian Surfels, FLAME/INSTA-style warping, multiresolution hash grids, residual embeddings, and threshold-based pruning. The new problem formulation and integration are valuable, but stronger controlled evidence is needed to demonstrate that the proposed components, rather than data sharing and capacity, yield the advertised capabilities.

Dataset governance is not yet adequate for such identity-sensitive material. The collection uses celebrity YouTube videos and movie footage, but provenance, copyright authorization, consent, annotation methodology, demographic labeling, and removal procedures are not specified. A non-commercial license and access agreement alone do not resolve these concerns, and the blank project-page reference plus promised future safeguards weaken reproducibility and confidence in dataset availability.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and underexplored computer-vision problem: constructing controllable 3D head avatars from unstructured photographs spanning multiple life stages, rather than from a single capture session.

TimeWalker is a reasonably coherent system that combines a shared canonical representation, stage-dependent neural bases, and FLAME-guided dynamic 2D Gaussian surfels. It supports rendering, expression transfer, viewpoint changes, and mesh extraction within one framework.

The reported image-reconstruction results are promising: TimeWalker substantially improves PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over several adapted baselines under the authors' evaluation protocols. The supplementary material also includes component ablations, comparisons to generative and one-shot methods, runtime information, failure cases, and qualitative results across several identities.

The proposed TimeWalker-1.0 collection is potentially useful: it contains 40 identities and 2.7M in-the-wild frames with substantial variation in age, pose, illumination, appearance, and accessories. The paper also acknowledges important limitations involving extreme poses, expressions, unseen mouth regions, preprocessing errors, and incomplete age coverage.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the central scientific claims are not adequately validated. The paper claims lifelong identity consistency, disentangled control, temporal interpolation, accurate geometry, and expression generalization, but its principal evaluation consists of per-frame PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on held-out frames. There is no systematic evaluation of age accuracy, cross-age identity preservation, expression fidelity, temporal consistency, disentanglement, or interpolation to genuinely unobserved life stages.

The train/test construction is concerning: the last 10% of frames from each appearance is used for testing, but the manuscript does not establish separation by source video or capture event. Neighboring frames from Internet videos can be nearly duplicates, so this split may substantially overestimate novel-view and generalization performance. A source-video-disjoint protocol is necessary.

The evaluation covers only five of the dataset's 40 identities, with ablations on three identities. No per-identity results, uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or statistical tests are provided. The very small improvement of Dynamo over fixed alternatives—for example, 27.20 versus 26.94 PSNR and tied 0.077 LPIPS—does not convincingly support the claimed advantage of adaptive basis selection.

Baseline evidence is uneven. The closest prior work, PAV, is replaced by the authors' INSTA++ approximation because code is unavailable. Gaussian-Surfels++ is likewise an author-created heuristic extension. The GPHM numbers come from non-identical data and settings, and the INSTA-dataset experiment treats nine different people as nine 'appearances' of one person, which does not test lifelong modeling and confounds identity with life stage. Model capacity, storage, and total training cost are also omitted from the one-model-versus-many-model comparison.

Geometry is a major claimed contribution, yet mesh quality is assessed almost entirely through selected visual examples. There are no Chamfer distance, normal-consistency, landmark, or expression-deformation measurements against reliable geometry. The comparison additionally gives the static baselines only one life stage while the proposed method receives all stages, making it impossible to isolate the benefit of DNA-2DGS from that of additional data.

The 'lifelong' framing is overstated relative to the demonstrated evidence. The dataset reportedly spans approximately ages 20–80 and the evaluated identities contain only 8–13 discrete stages; the authors explicitly acknowledge that infancy through old age is not covered. Claimed generation of missing intermediate ages is asserted but not quantitatively or perceptually evaluated.

Important method details remain ambiguous. Dynamo's pruning rule is not specified precisely enough to reproduce, the constraints or normalization applied to blending weights are unclear, and the architecture of the deformation/color networks, stage formation and annotation, preprocessing models, data deduplication, and source-wise splits are insufficiently documented. The promised code and restricted dataset release are not available as evidence within the submission.

The dataset raises unresolved reproducibility and governance issues. It is scraped from YouTube and films and contains identifiable celebrities, but the manuscript does not clearly document source licenses, consent, copyright basis, annotation procedures, demographic definitions, duplicate removal, or a concrete access protocol. A future non-commercial agreement alone does not resolve these concerns.

Qualitative results reveal noticeable failures in hair and head boundaries, large viewpoints beyond roughly 45 degrees, lighting disentanglement, tongues, teeth, and exaggerated expressions. These are substantive for a method advertised as a realistic full-head avatar with full-scale animation, and no user study or perceptual evaluation establishes that the outputs maintain identity and realism across stages.

The presentation contains frequent grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology and table references, and unsupported causal interpretations—for example, inferring that fewer retained bases necessarily represent reusable identity characteristics. These issues make the method and experimental conclusions harder to assess precisely.

strengths: The paper introduces a compelling and underexplored computer-vision problem: constructing a controllable 3D head avatar from an individual's unstructured photographs spanning many life stages. This is a meaningful extension beyond momentary avatar reconstruction.

TimeWalker combines a shared canonical representation, neural head bases, adaptive basis pruning (Dynamo), and FLAME-driven dynamic 2D Gaussian surfels in a coherent framework supporting appearance, expression, shape, pose, and viewpoint control.

The reported rendering results are strong. On TimeWalker-1.0, the method substantially improves the one-model-per-identity comparison over INSTA++, INSTA, and FlashAvatar, reaching 27.28 PSNR, 0.949 SSIM, and 0.071 LPIPS. Similar trends on the public INSTA data provide useful corroborating evidence.

The qualitative results across ages, identities, reenactment settings, and viewpoints are generally convincing, especially for frontal and moderate-pose rendering. The method also produces substantially cleaner meshes than the illustrated COLMAP, Gaussian-Surfels, and INSTA++ alternatives.

The ablations cover the principal components. Removing Dynamo or restricting the model to one hashgrid causes a clear degradation, while the residual-embedding and geometry-loss studies help explain their respective effects on rendering and mesh quality.

TimeWalker-1.0 is potentially valuable: it contains 2.7 million frames for 40 identities, with varied ages, expressions, poses, ethnicities, accessories, and illumination. The authors describe its collection and filtering pipeline and provide useful distribution analyses.

The paper is unusually comprehensive, with comparisons to reconstruction, generative, and one-shot avatar approaches; computational-cost information; downstream editing examples; explicit failure cases; and a thoughtful discussion of limitations and misuse risks.
weaknesses: The evaluation split may substantially overestimate generalization. The data are extracted from videos, yet the last 10% of frames from each appearance are used for testing. Temporally neighboring frames can be nearly duplicates and share background, lighting, and motion. A split by source video, event, or acquisition session is needed.

Although the dataset contains 40 identities, the main quantitative evaluation uses only five selected identities, and ablations use three. Identity consistency is evaluated on only three identities. Broader per-identity results, variance, and selection criteria are needed to substantiate robustness.

The central claims of a disentangled lifelong space are not directly validated. There is no quantitative test of held-out life stages, age interpolation, age ordering, or independent manipulation of age versus hairstyle, accessories, illumination, and body-weight changes. Learned lifestage codes may therefore memorize appearance clusters rather than form a meaningful temporal axis.

Dynamo's technical justification is incomplete. Because basis features and blending weights can be rescaled jointly, pruning bases solely when their weights fall below a threshold is not clearly identifiable without normalization or other constraints. Moreover, its improvement over using all hashgrids is modest (27.20 versus 26.86 PSNR, with identical reported LPIPS), so claims of superior generalization are stronger than the evidence supports.

Geometry is assessed primarily through qualitative mesh renderings. There are no surface-distance, normal, landmark, temporal-consistency, or expression-transfer measurements against 3D ground truth. Thus, the claimed geometric accuracy and dynamic-mesh advantages remain less convincingly established than rendering quality.

Baseline fairness is mixed. INSTA++ and Gaussian-Surfels++ are author-created adaptations, PAV is represented through a reimplementation rather than its original system, and several baselines are not designed for multi-lifestage modeling. Parameter count, storage, and total training cost for one TimeWalker model versus the collection of per-stage models are also omitted.

The term “lifelong” is somewhat overstated: the dataset reportedly covers approximately ages 20–80 and the authors acknowledge that it does not span infancy to old age. Performance also degrades beyond roughly 45-degree yaw, under exaggerated expressions, and for unseen mouth structures such as the tongue.

Reproducibility and data governance need strengthening. Important details of defining and labeling lifestages are unclear, and the large dataset consists of celebrity footage sourced from YouTube and movies. A non-commercial data-use agreement is helpful but does not by itself resolve consent, copyright, identity misuse, or demographic-bias concerns.
